title: Unification of Upper and Lower Egypt
summary: Around 3100 BC a ruler remembered as Narmer (often identified with Menes) brought the Nile valley and the Delta under a single crown, founding Egypt's First Dynasty. The Narmer Palette, showing the king wearing both the white and red crowns, is the oldest surviving image of that union.

title: Cuneiform writing in Sumer
summary: In the temple cities of southern Mesopotamia, above all Uruk, scribes pressed reed styluses into clay to record grain, livestock and debts. By about 3000 BC those tallies had become cuneiform, the first full writing system, and with it the first written law, literature and history.

title: The Great Pyramid of Giza is built
summary: Pharaoh Khufu's tomb on the Giza plateau was completed around 2560 BC after roughly two decades of work by a rotating state labour force. At about 146 metres it remained the tallest structure built by humans for some 3,800 years and is the only one of the seven ancient wonders still standing.

title: Mature Indus Valley cities flourish
summary: From about 2600 BC the Harappan civilisation built brick cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa across the Indus basin, with gridded streets, covered drains and standardised weights. Its script has never been deciphered, and the cities were largely abandoned after 1900 BC.

title: Minoan palaces of Crete
summary: From around 2000 BC the Minoans built sprawling palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, decorated with frescoes of bulls, dolphins and processions. Europe's first advanced civilisation traded across the Aegean until a combination of the Thera eruption and Mycenaean takeover ended it after 1450 BC.

title: Hammurabi's law code
summary: King Hammurabi of Babylon had some 282 rulings carved onto a two-metre diorite stele around 1754 BC, covering wages, marriage, medicine and retaliation. It is the longest surviving law collection from the ancient Near East and fixed the idea that a king's justice should be publicly readable.

title: The Olmec rise on the Gulf coast
summary: From about 1200 BC the Olmec built ceremonial centres at San Lorenzo and later La Venta in the swampy Gulf lowlands, carving colossal basalt heads up to three metres high. Their calendar, ballgame and rain deity shaped every later Mesoamerican culture, earning them the name 'mother culture'.

title: Battle of Kadesh
summary: Ramesses II of Egypt and Muwatalli II of the Hittites fought the largest chariot battle known to history on the Orontes in 1274 BC. Neither side won outright, and the treaty that followed some fifteen years later is the earliest surviving international peace agreement.

title: The Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within a few decades around 1200–1150 BC the Hittite empire fell, Ugarit and Mycenae burned, and Egypt barely repelled the Sea Peoples. Drought, earthquakes, migration and the breakdown of palace trade networks combined into the first recorded systems collapse, and literacy vanished from Greece for centuries.

title: Kush conquers Egypt
summary: The Nubian kingdom of Kush, ruling from Napata on the middle Nile, pushed north under Piye and Shabaka and governed all Egypt as its 25th Dynasty from about 747 BC. The 'black pharaohs' restored old temples and built steep-sided pyramids at El-Kurru and later Meroë.

title: Traditional founding of Rome
summary: Roman tradition dated the founding of the city on the Palatine Hill to 21 April 753 BC, ascribing it to Romulus. Archaeology shows Iron Age huts on the hill from roughly that era, and the legendary date became the anchor of the Roman calendar, counted ab urbe condita.

title: First recorded Olympic Games
summary: The Greeks dated their first Olympiad at Olympia to 776 BC, when Koroibos of Elis won the stadion foot race. Held every four years in honour of Zeus under a sacred truce, the games became the shared calendar of a politically fragmented Greek world.

title: Cyrus the Great takes Babylon
summary: In October 539 BC Cyrus II of Persia entered Babylon after defeating Nabonidus, completing the largest empire the world had yet seen. The Cyrus Cylinder records his restoration of local cults, and the Hebrew Bible credits him with allowing the exiled Judeans to return to Jerusalem.

title: Darius I begins Persepolis
summary: Around 518 BC Darius the Great began a ceremonial capital on a terrace in Fars, with the Apadana audience hall and staircases carved with tribute-bearers from every satrapy. Persepolis was the Achaemenid empire's showpiece until Alexander's army burned it in 330 BC.

title: Cleisthenes founds Athenian democracy
summary: After the tyrants were expelled, Cleisthenes reorganised Athens in 508–507 BC into ten artificial tribes, giving every adult male citizen a vote in the assembly and a place in the council of 500. It was the first system to put sovereignty in the hands of ordinary citizens rather than a king or aristocracy.

title: Battle of Marathon
summary: In 490 BC roughly 10,000 Athenians and Plataeans under Miltiades charged and broke a larger Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon. The victory saved the young Athenian democracy and entered legend through the runner who carried news of it to the city.

title: The Buddha's enlightenment at Bodh Gaya
summary: Siddhartha Gautama, a prince of the Shakya clan, is held to have reached awakening beneath a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya in the fifth century BC and then taught the four noble truths at Sarnath. Buddhism spread from the Ganges plain to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China and Japan.

title: Confucius teaches in Lu
summary: Kong Qiu, an unsuccessful official from the state of Lu, spent his later life teaching ritual propriety, filial duty and government by moral example. His students' record of his sayings, the Analects, became the backbone of Chinese education and bureaucracy for two millennia.

title: Alexander defeats Darius at Gaugamela
summary: On 1 October 331 BC Alexander of Macedon broke the Persian centre at Gaugamela, and Darius III fled. Within two years the Achaemenid empire was his, and Greek language, coinage and city planning reached from Egypt to the Indus in the Hellenistic age that followed.

title: Ashoka renounces war after Kalinga
summary: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka conquered Kalinga around 261 BC at a cost he put at 100,000 dead, and by his own account turned to Buddhist dhamma in remorse. He had edicts on tolerance, welfare and non-violence carved on rocks and pillars from Afghanistan to southern India.

title: The Punic Wars begin
summary: Rome and Carthage fought three wars between 264 and 146 BC for control of the western Mediterranean, including Hannibal's march over the Alps and Scipio's victory at Zama. The final war ended with Carthage razed, leaving Rome without a rival at sea.

title: Qin Shi Huang unifies China
summary: In 221 BC the king of Qin defeated the last of the warring states and declared himself First Emperor, standardising script, coinage, weights and axle widths. His short dynasty built early walls in the north and the terracotta army at Xi'an, and set the template of a unified Chinese state.

title: Zhang Qian opens the Silk Road
summary: The Han envoy Zhang Qian returned from thirteen years in Central Asia with the first Chinese reports of Ferghana, Bactria and Parthia. The trade routes that opened after him carried silk west and horses, glass, Buddhism and disease east for the next 1,500 years.

title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
summary: On 10 January 49 BC Julius Caesar led the Thirteenth Legion across the small river marking the boundary of his province, an act of war against the Senate. The civil war that followed destroyed the Republic and ended with his dictatorship and assassination in 44 BC.

title: Augustus founds the Roman Empire
summary: In January 27 BC the Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus and a bundle of powers that made him princeps in all but name. His forty-year rule ended a century of civil war and began the Pax Romana, two centuries of relative peace across the Mediterranean world.

title: The crucifixion of Jesus
summary: Jesus of Nazareth, a Galilean preacher, was executed in Jerusalem under the prefect Pontius Pilate around AD 30–33. His followers' conviction that he had risen turned a Jewish movement into a faith that within four centuries was the official religion of the Roman Empire.

title: Teotihuacan becomes a great city
summary: In the Valley of Mexico, Teotihuacan grew from the first century AD into a planned city of perhaps 125,000 people along the Avenue of the Dead, with the vast Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. Its builders left no readable name for themselves; the Aztecs, finding it in ruins, called it the place where the gods were made.

title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
summary: In AD 79 Vesuvius erupted for some eighteen hours, burying Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pyroclastic surges and killing thousands. Pliny the Younger's letters describe the column of smoke, and the sealed towns preserved Roman daily life in extraordinary detail.
wikipediaTitle: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD

title: Aksum becomes a trading power
summary: The Ethiopian kingdom of Aksum controlled Red Sea trade between Rome and India, minted its own gold coinage and raised granite stelae up to 24 metres tall. Around AD 330 King Ezana converted to Christianity, making Aksum one of the earliest Christian states.

title: Constantine founds Constantinople
summary: On 11 May 330 Constantine dedicated the rebuilt Greek town of Byzantium as his New Rome on the Bosporus. Its walls and position made it the richest city in Christendom and the capital of a Roman state that survived for another eleven centuries.

title: Classic Maya cities at their height
summary: Between roughly AD 250 and 900 rival Maya city-states such as Tikal, Calakmul and Palenque raised limestone pyramids and recorded dynastic history in a fully phonetic glyph script. Their astronomers tracked Venus and ran a calendar accurate to the day over millennia before drought and war emptied the lowland cities.

title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: On 4 September 476 the Germanic commander Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. No new western emperor was appointed, and the date became the conventional end of antiquity in Europe.
wikipediaTitle: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

title: Justinian builds the Hagia Sophia
summary: Justinian I had the burnt cathedral of Constantinople rebuilt in under six years, and its 31-metre dome on pendentives was dedicated on 27 December 537. The largest interior space in the world for nearly a thousand years, it served in turn as cathedral, mosque and museum.

title: The Plague of Justinian
summary: Bubonic plague reached Constantinople from Egypt in 541 and spread around the Mediterranean in waves for two centuries. Contemporary writers describe thousands of deaths a day in the capital, and the losses crippled Justinian's attempt to reconquer the western empire.

title: The Hijra and the rise of Islam
summary: In 622 Muhammad and his followers left Mecca for Yathrib, which became Medina, and formed the first Muslim community there. The year of that migration starts the Islamic calendar, and within a century Arab armies carrying the new faith ruled from Spain to the Indus.

title: Battle of the Yarmuk
summary: In August 636 Arab forces under Khalid ibn al-Walid destroyed a large Byzantine army on the Yarmuk river south of Damascus. Syria and Palestine passed permanently out of Roman hands, and the shape of the Middle East was set for the next thirteen centuries.

title: Tang Chang'an, the world's largest city
summary: Under the Tang, Chang'an grew into a walled grid of perhaps a million people, the eastern terminus of the Silk Road and home to Nestorian, Zoroastrian and Buddhist communities. Its poets Li Bai and Du Fu and its block-printed books mark a high point of Chinese civilisation.

title: Al-Mansur founds Baghdad
summary: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur laid out a circular capital on the Tigris in 762, and within a century Baghdad was the largest city on earth. Its House of Wisdom translated Greek, Persian and Indian science into Arabic, preserving and extending it through al-Khwarizmi's algebra and Arabic numerals.

title: Viking raid on Lindisfarne
summary: On 8 June 793 Norse raiders sacked the island monastery of Lindisfarne off Northumbria, shocking Christian Europe. The raid opened three centuries in which Scandinavians raided, traded and settled from Dublin and Normandy to Kyiv, Iceland and Newfoundland.

title: Charlemagne crowned emperor
summary: On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned the Frankish king Charlemagne emperor in St Peter's, reviving an imperial title in the west after three centuries. His court at Aachen drove a revival of learning and set the long entanglement of pope and emperor in motion.

title: Borobudur is completed
summary: The Shailendra rulers of central Java finished a stepped stone mandala of nine platforms carrying more than 2,600 relief panels and 500 Buddha statues around 825. Abandoned after the centre of Javanese power moved east, Borobudur is the largest Buddhist monument in the world.

title: Suryavarman II builds Angkor Wat
summary: The Khmer king Suryavarman II raised a sandstone temple-mountain to Vishnu at his capital Angkor in the first half of the twelfth century. The largest religious structure ever built, it anchored a city whose canals and reservoirs supported perhaps three quarters of a million people.

title: Srivijaya controls the straits
summary: From Palembang on Sumatra, the Buddhist maritime state of Srivijaya taxed shipping through the Malacca and Sunda straits for some six centuries. Chinese pilgrims stopped there to study Sanskrit, and its fleets made it the dominant power of island Southeast Asia until Chola raids in 1025.

title: Battle of Hastings
summary: On 14 October 1066 William, Duke of Normandy, defeated and killed King Harold Godwinson near Hastings and went on to be crowned in London. The Norman conquest replaced the English aristocracy, reshaped the language and tied England to continental politics for centuries.

title: The First Crusade takes Jerusalem
summary: Pope Urban II called western knights to the east at Clermont in 1095, and in July 1099 the crusaders stormed Jerusalem and massacred much of its population. Four crusader states were founded in the Levant, beginning two centuries of holy war and of sharpened contact between Latin Europe and Islam.

title: Song China's commercial revolution
summary: Song China issued the world's first government paper money, ran blast furnaces producing iron on a scale Europe would not match for centuries, and used the magnetic compass at sea. Kaifeng and later Hangzhou were the largest and richest cities on earth.

title: Magna Carta sealed at Runnymede
summary: Facing baronial revolt, King John sealed a charter of liberties in a meadow by the Thames on 15 June 1215, accepting that the king was bound by law. Annulled within weeks, it was reissued repeatedly and became the founding text invoked for due process and trial by peers.

title: Genghis Khan proclaimed
summary: At a kurultai on the Onon river in 1206 Temüjin was acclaimed Genghis Khan, ruler of all the felt-tent peoples of the steppe. He reorganised the tribes into a decimal army under a written law, and within seventy years his heirs governed the largest contiguous land empire in history.

title: Mongols sack Zhongdu
summary: After a long siege the Mongols took the Jin capital Zhongdu, on the site of modern Beijing, in June 1215 and burned much of it. The victory gave Genghis Khan Chinese siege engineers and administrators and opened the long conquest of northern China.

title: Siege of Baghdad
summary: Hulagu Khan's army broke into Baghdad in February 1258, killed the last Abbasid caliph and destroyed the libraries and canals of the city. The sack ended five centuries of Abbasid authority and is remembered as a catastrophe for Islamic learning.

title: Battle of Ain Jalut
summary: On 3 September 1260 the Mamluk army of Egypt under Qutuz and Baybars defeated a Mongol force in the Jezreel valley. It was the first serious check to Mongol expansion westward and left Egypt and the holy cities in Mamluk hands.

title: Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty
summary: In 1271 Kublai proclaimed a Chinese-style dynasty, the Yuan, from his capital Dadu on the site of Beijing, completing the conquest of the Song by 1279. For the first time China was ruled entirely by a steppe dynasty, and travellers such as Marco Polo crossed a continent under one peace.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca
summary: The Mali emperor Mansa Musa crossed the Sahara to Mecca in 1324 with a caravan of thousands, spending so much gold in Cairo that its value reportedly fell for years. His journey put Mali and the scholarly city of Timbuktu on European maps for the first time.

title: Great Zimbabwe at its height
summary: On the Zimbabwe plateau a Shona kingdom built dry-stone walls up to eleven metres high without mortar, enclosing a town of perhaps 18,000 people. Chinese porcelain and Persian glass found there show it traded gold and ivory to the Swahili coast and beyond.

title: The Black Death sweeps Eurasia
summary: Plague arrived at Messina on Genoese galleys in October 1347 and within four years killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's people, after already devastating Central Asia and the Middle East. Labour shortages broke serfdom in the west and reshaped wages, religion and art for generations.

title: The Ming drive out the Yuan
summary: After decades of famine, flooding and Red Turban rebellion, the peasant-born Zhu Yuanzhang proclaimed the Ming dynasty at Nanjing in 1368 and took Dadu that autumn. The Mongol court withdrew to the steppe, ending the last unified Mongol rule of China.
